name: README.md
label: Read me first
text:
# gridmind

A hands-on lab for constraint satisfaction and machine learning. Grid puzzles
are the vehicle; the subject is how a machine reasons — by rules, by learning,
or by both.

50 lessons across 9 stages, from a hand-written backtracking solver to a
neural network, to a hybrid of the two, to a roster scheduler and a model
running in the browser. Tagged by what each one actually teaches: 25 ML,
11 Classical AI, 6 Engineering, 5 Frontend, 3 Computer Vision. See
[CURRICULUM.md](CURRICULUM.md).

New here? Read [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) — why the project is built this way,
what has been measured, and what to do when something does not work.

**Live demo:** https://sks-balan.github.io/gridmind-demo/ — the browser app,
published as a static site. Note that it bundles this repo's docs, lessons and
source into itself, so deploying the demo publishes that content even though
this repo is private. `scripts/deploy-demo.sh` rebuilds and republishes it;
`--dry-run` builds without publishing.

## Works offline

This is a hard requirement of the project, not a nice-to-have. Everything
needed is already on disk:

- **Dependencies** are installed in `.venv/` (torch, torchvision, OpenCV,
  scikit-learn, ONNX Runtime, python-sat, OR-Tools, JupyterLab).
- **Training data is generated, not downloaded.** The solver in
  `src/gridmind/generate.py` is an unlimited source of labelled puzzles, so
  Stages 0–3 and 5–7 never need a network.
- **MNIST is pre-cached** in `data/raw/` for Stage 4. It is the only external
  dataset in the entire curriculum.

Verify at any time, with the network off:

```bash
.venv/bin/gridmind selfcheck
```

## Setup

Already done — but if you ever need to rebuild the environment:

```bash
uv venv --python 3.13 && uv pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

Python 3.13 specifically: PyTorch has no wheels for 3.14 yet, which is what
`python3` resolves to on this machine.

## Opening in VS Code

```bash
code ~/development/gridmind
```

The interpreter, pytest integration and two debug configurations are already
committed in `.vscode/`. Select the `.venv` interpreter if prompted, then hit
F5 to step through the solver.

## Quick start

```bash
.venv/bin/gridmind selfcheck
```

```bash
.venv/bin/gridmind solve --puzzle 000260701680070090190004500820100040004602900050003028009300074040050036703018000
```

```bash
.venv/bin/gridmind generate --count 3 --clues 26
```

```bash
.venv/bin/gridmind bench --count 50 --clues 26
```

```bash
.venv/bin/gridmind dataset --count 5000 --augment 4 --out data/train.npz
```

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests -q
```

## A first walk through

Nothing below needs a network connection.

**1. Confirm the install.** Every subsystem, end to end:

```bash
.venv/bin/gridmind selfcheck
```

**2. Watch the solver work.** This puzzle needs real search — constraint
propagation alone will not finish it:

```bash
.venv/bin/gridmind solve --puzzle 000000000302540000050301070000000004409006005023054790000000050700810000080060009
```

Look at the `stats` line it prints. `nodes` is how many times the solver had to
guess. That number is the currency of Stage 0 — every heuristic you add in
Lesson 05 is judged by how far it drives it down.

**3. See where propagation stops being enough.** Now try a puzzle that
propagation solves outright, and compare the node count:

```bash
.venv/bin/gridmind solve --puzzle 000260701680070090190004500820100040004602900050003028009300074040050036703018000
```

Zero nodes. No guessing at all. The gap between these two puzzles is what
Lessons 03 through 05 are about.

**4. Generate your own data.** This is the engine that makes the repo work
offline:

```bash
.venv/bin/gridmind generate --count 3 --clues 26
```

**5. Measure.** Fifty puzzles, with the node distribution:

```bash
.venv/bin/gridmind bench --count 50 --clues 26
```

**6. Open it in VS Code and start Lesson 01.**

```bash
code ~/development/gridmind
```

Then read [`lessons/01_board_representation/README.md`](lessons/01_board_representation/README.md).
It is written out in full as the template for what a worked lesson looks like;
the rest have objectives and tasks, and get fleshed out as you reach them.

Press F5 to debug — `.vscode/launch.json` has configurations that break into
the solver and the dataset builder. Set a breakpoint in
`src/gridmind/propagate.py` and step through `hidden_singles` once; it is the
fastest way to understand what propagation actually does.

## The browser app

The whole curriculum is also browsable in a local web app, alongside a working
solver you can watch think.

```bash
cd ~/development/gridmind && scripts/server.sh start
```

Then open **http://localhost:5174**. Stop it with `scripts/server.sh stop`;
`status`, `restart`, `logs` and `attach` also work. It runs detached, so it
survives closing the terminal and laptop sleep, and `start` is safe to run
twice. Override the port with `GRIDMIND_PORT=5175`.

Four views:

- **Solver** — enter or paste a puzzle, solve it, and see the node count. Turn
  on candidates to watch constraint propagation, or hit **Animate** to replay
  the search step by step: blue for inferred cells, orange for guesses, with
  cells clearing again on backtrack.
- **Lessons** — all 50 lessons, grouped by stage and tagged by kind, with the
  tasks and theory rendered inline.
- **Docs** — this README, [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md), [CURRICULUM.md](CURRICULUM.md)
  and [COMMANDS.md](COMMANDS.md), rendered in the app.
- **Code** — every source file in the repo, filterable, in a read-only
  CodeMirror editor: syntax highlighting, line numbers, folding and Cmd-F
  search, with IDE-style open-file tabs. Python library, tests, tooling,
  lesson demos and the TypeScript browser code.

The Docs and Code tabs read JSON bundles generated alongside the lessons, so
**they go stale when you edit source**. Refresh them with:

```bash
cd ~/development/gridmind && source .env && python tools/scaffold_lessons.py
```

`web/src/core/` is a TypeScript port of the Python solver and produces
identical node counts — 3 on the hard reference puzzle, 0 on the easy one.
Proving that parity is Lesson 45.

Dependencies are already installed in `web/node_modules`, so this works
offline. `npm run build` produces a static `dist/` you can host anywhere.

## What is built already

Stage 0's reference implementation is complete and tested (30 tests). It is
the code Lessons 01–08 read, measure and extend.

| Module | What it holds |
|--------|---------------|
| `units.py` | Cells, units, peers, the constraint graph (81 nodes, 810 edges) |
| `board.py` | Parsing, rendering, conflict detection, validation |
| `propagate.py` | Bitmask domains, naked singles, hidden singles, AC-3 |
| `solvers/backtracking.py` | Search with MRV/LCV, instrumented, pluggable heuristics |
| `generate.py` | Random grids, uniqueness-preserving digging |
| `augment.py` | The symmetry group — 1.2 trillion variants of any grid |
| `dataset.py` | Dataset building, grouped splits, leakage-free by default |
| `metrics.py` | Cell vs grid accuracy, breakdowns by clue count |

Lessons 01–11 additionally have full theory notes and working `run.py`
demos. Lessons 12–50 have folders, objectives, concepts, tasks and success
criteria, and their `run.py` prints the brief — but the implementation is
yours to write. That is the point.

Two hooks in the solver exist specifically for later stages:
`select_var` and `order_values` in `solvers/backtracking.py` let a learned
policy replace a hand-written heuristic without touching the search, which is
what Stage 3 does.

## Layout

```
src/gridmind/     reference implementation
lessons/NN_slug/  one folder per lesson: README, your code, your notes
tools/            lesson manifest and scaffolding
tests/            the suite that must pass before any ML lesson
data/             generated datasets and cached MNIST (gitignored)
```

## Editing the curriculum

Lesson content lives in `tools/lesson_manifest.py`. Edit there, then:

```bash
.venv/bin/python tools/scaffold_lessons.py
```

It regenerates `CURRICULUM.md` and creates any missing lesson folders. It will
not overwrite a README you have already written in — pass `--force` if you
really mean to.

## Three things worth knowing before you start

**Grid accuracy, not cell accuracy.** A model that fills 80% of cells
correctly solves almost no puzzles: 0.8 to the power of 50 is a rounding error.
Every result in this repo reports both, and the second one is the real one.

**Split by group, never by row.** Augmented copies of one base grid are not
independent samples. `dataset.split_by_group` handles it; `naive_split` exists
only so Lesson 11 can show you the size of the lie.

**Measure in nodes, not seconds.** When Stage 3 puts a neural network inside
the search loop, wall-clock time mostly measures Python overhead. Node count
is what tells you whether the model actually helped.

name: DESIGN.md
label: Design notes
text:
# Design notes

Why this project is built the way it is, what has been measured, and what to do
when something does not work. Read this after the README and before Lesson 01.

## The idea this rests on

A sudoku solver is an **oracle**. Give it a puzzle and it returns the one
correct answer, exactly, every time.

That is unusual, and it is what makes constraint puzzles such a good vehicle
for learning machine learning. Most ML projects die at data collection: you
need labelled examples, labels are expensive, and the ones you get are noisy.
Here, labels are free and perfect. `src/gridmind/generate.py` produces as many
`(puzzle, solution)` pairs as you want, and every label is provably correct
because the generator checks that each puzzle has exactly one solution.

Two consequences run through the whole curriculum:

- **You can always measure.** Every model is scored against ground truth, and
  a classical solver sits alongside it as a baseline that is exact and instant.
  A neural network that solves fewer puzzles than plain constraint propagation
  has learned nothing worth having, and you will know immediately.
- **Nothing needs the internet.** Data is generated, not downloaded.

## Why sudoku, and why not only sudoku

Sudoku is a constraint satisfaction problem, and a small one. The same
machinery — variables, domains, constraints, propagation, search — solves
n-queens, graph colouring, Latin squares, and then staff rostering, timetabling
and scheduling, which are problems organisations pay to have solved.

Stage 6 makes that explicit by pointing the same solver at those problems. The
9×9 grid is a teaching surface, not the subject.

## Why the later stages are unfinished

This is a curriculum, not a library. Stage 0 is complete, tested and correct,
because you need something dependable to read and to measure against. From
Stage 2 onward the implementations are exercises — the folder, the objective,
the concepts, the tasks and the success criteria are there, and the code is
yours to write.

Reading a finished neural sudoku solver teaches you much less than building one
that plateaus at 25 clues and working out why.

## Why half the lessons are not machine learning

Of 50 lessons: 25 ML, 11 classical AI, 6 engineering, 5 frontend, 3 computer
vision. The non-ML half is not filler.

A real machine learning project is mostly the scaffolding that makes results
mean anything: how data is represented, how it is split, what is measured, and
what the baseline is. Stage 0 exists so that when a model in Stage 2 claims to
beat something, the claim is checkable. Every lesson is tagged with its kind so
you always know which skill you are practising.

## The three principles

These recur in every stage and matter more than any individual lesson.

**Grid accuracy, not cell accuracy.** A model that fills 80% of cells correctly
solves almost no puzzles — `0.8^50` is about 1.4 × 10⁻⁵. Report both, and treat
the second as the real one.

**Split by group, never by row.** Augmented copies of one base grid are not
independent samples. `dataset.split_by_group` handles this; `naive_split`
exists only so Lesson 11 can show you how large the resulting overestimate is.

**Measure in nodes, not seconds.** Once a neural network sits inside the search
loop, wall-clock time mostly measures Python overhead. Node count — how many
times the solver had to guess — is what tells you whether the model helped.

## Measured baselines

Run on an Apple Silicon laptop, Python 3.13, CPU for the solver:

| | |
|---|---|
| Reference hard puzzle | 3 nodes, ~1.3 ms |
| Reference easy puzzle | 0 nodes — propagation alone finishes it |
| TypeScript port | identical node counts to Python |
| Test suite | 30 tests |
| Puzzle library | 62 puzzles, 22–36 clues, 0–7 nodes |

That last row is worth dwelling on. Across 62 generated puzzles, 46 need no
search at all, and the hardest needs only seven guesses. Constraint propagation
is *that* strong — and the library contains 24-clue puzzles needing zero search
alongside 30-clue puzzles needing several. Clue count is a weak difficulty
proxy, which is the subject of Lesson 31, visible in the data before you get
there.

## Bugs found while building this, kept as lessons

**The parser treated `-` as an empty cell.** `render()` draws box separators
with `-`, so a rendered grid parsed back as 99 cells instead of 81. Caught by a
round-trip test asserting `from_string(render(b)) == b`. Keep that test.

**Box borders were drawn one row too low.** A CSS `nth-child` range off by nine
cells. Invisible in code review, obvious the moment anyone looked at the page.

**A test asserted something false.** The original suite claimed hidden singles
would outperform naked singles on the easy reference puzzle. They do not —
naked singles alone finish it. The test now uses the hard puzzle, where hidden
singles genuinely reduce undecided cells from 54 to 50. Check assumptions
against data before turning them into assertions.

## Where you are likely to get stuck

**Lesson 05 — MRV looks unimpressive.** At 24 clues, MRV barely beats
first-empty-cell, because propagation is doing nearly all the work. Generate
harder puzzles (20–22 clues) or disable propagation so search has to earn its
keep. The heuristic's value is dramatic once propagation stops masking it.

**Lesson 12 — the training loop will not learn.** Overfit a single batch of
eight puzzles to ~100% first. If it cannot, the loop is broken and the bug is
in the loss, the masking, or the target indexing — cross-entropy targets must
be zero-indexed, so digit `d` becomes class `d-1`. Never debug this on the full
dataset.

**Lesson 17 — iterative decoding does not help.** Check that you re-run the
model after each filled cell rather than reusing the first forward pass, and
that you pick the most confident *empty* cell.

**Stage 3 — the learned heuristic loses to MRV.** That is a legitimate result.
MRV is strong and nearly free. The real question is whether guidance pays off
at difficulty levels where search actually explodes.

**Lesson 30 — end-to-end accuracy collapses.** Expected: 99% per digit across
~30 clues is `0.99^30`, about 74% per puzzle. The fix is the thesis of the
whole repo — use the solver to detect the failure and revisit the
lowest-confidence digits.

**Anywhere.** Run `gridmind selfcheck` and `pytest tests -q`. If those pass,
the foundation is sound and the problem is in your new code.

## What is deliberately not here

- Theory notes for Lessons 12–50. Lessons 01–11 are written out in full and set
  the intended depth; the rest list their concepts as a syllabus. Writing your
  own is better learning than reading someone else's.
- `run.py` demos for Lessons 12–50. They execute and print the brief; the
  implementation is the exercise.
- `src/gridmind/solvers/dlx.py`. Lesson 06 builds the 729×324 incidence
  structure for you; Algorithm X and dancing links are yours.
- `web/src/ml/`. Lessons 48 and 49.

## A suggested order

1. **Stage 0 (01–08)** — move quickly if constraint solving is familiar, but
   build the benchmark harness in Lesson 08 properly. Everything later depends
   on it.
2. **Stage 1 (09–11)** — short. Lesson 11 is the most broadly transferable
   lesson here.
3. **Stage 2 (12–19)** — the core ML work. Lesson 17 is the payoff.
4. **Stage 8 (43–47)** — good to interleave. Visualising the solver makes
   Stages 0 and 3 concrete, and it is a change of pace from training loops.
5. **Stage 3 (20–24)** — the neurosymbolic material, and the most original.
6. **Stage 4 (25–30)** — self-contained; a computer vision detour.
7. **Stages 5–7** — difficulty modelling, generalisation, deployment.

name: CURRICULUM.md
label: Curriculum
text:
# Curriculum

50 lessons in 9 stages: 25 ML, 11 Classical AI, 6 Engineering, 5 Frontend, 3 Computer Vision.

Generated from `tools/lesson_manifest.py` — edit that, then run
`.venv/bin/python tools/scaffold_lessons.py`.

Every lesson folder holds a `README.md` (tasks), a `THEORY.md`
(background) and a runnable `run.py`. Work the stages in order: the
measurement discipline from Stage 0 is what makes every later claim
mean anything.

Browse them in the app instead: `cd web && npm run dev`.

## Stage 0 — Classical foundations

_How the problem is structured and solved by rules alone._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 01 | [Board representation and validation](lessons/01_board_representation/README.md) | Engineering | Settle how a puzzle is stored, parsed, printed and checked, because every later stage inherits this choice. |
| 02 | [Units, peers, and the constraint graph](lessons/02_units_and_peers/README.md) | Classical AI | Derive the structure of the puzzle once, and see sudoku for what it is: graph colouring on a 20-regular graph. |
| 03 | [Constraint propagation: naked and hidden singles](lessons/03_constraint_propagation/README.md) | Classical AI | Implement the two inference rules that solve most puzzles without any search at all. |
| 04 | [Arc consistency (AC-3), and its limits](lessons/04_arc_consistency/README.md) | Classical AI | Implement the textbook algorithm, then discover it buys you nothing over naked singles here -- and understand exactly why. |
| 05 | [Backtracking search and its heuristics](lessons/05_backtracking_search/README.md) | Classical AI | Add search on top of propagation, then watch good heuristics cut the search tree by orders of magnitude. |
| 06 | [Exact cover: Algorithm X and dancing links](lessons/06_exact_cover_dlx/README.md) | Classical AI | Re-cast sudoku as an exact cover problem and implement Knuth's DLX, a completely different and very fast attack. |
| 07 | [Puzzle generation and uniqueness](lessons/07_puzzle_generation/README.md) | Classical AI | Build the data source the whole repo runs on: well-formed puzzles with exactly one solution. |
| 08 | [Benchmarking and difficulty proxies](lessons/08_benchmark_harness/README.md) | Engineering | Build the measurement discipline every later claim depends on. Nothing after this is believable without it. |

## Stage 1 — Data

_Turning a solver into an unlimited, honest data source._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 09 | [Tensors, encoding, and the shape of the problem](lessons/09_tensors_and_encoding/README.md) | ML | Move from numpy arrays to torch tensors and decide how a grid becomes model input. |
| 10 | [Symmetry augmentation](lessons/10_symmetry_augmentation/README.md) | ML | Exploit sudoku's symmetry group for near-free data, and understand precisely what that data is worth. |
| 11 | [Splits, grouping, and leakage](lessons/11_splits_and_leakage/README.md) | ML | Make the leakage mistake on purpose, measure how big a lie it tells, then fix it permanently. |

## Stage 2 — Supervised deep learning

_Teaching a network to fill the grid, and finding out where it stops._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 12 | [A training loop, written by hand](lessons/12_training_loop_from_scratch/README.md) | ML | Build an MLP baseline and write the loop yourself: forward, loss, backward, step. No framework helpers. |
| 13 | [Autograd, optimizers, and schedules](lessons/13_autograd_optimizers_schedules/README.md) | ML | Understand what the loop is actually doing, and how the knobs change it. |
| 14 | [Convolutions, and why they are a poor fit here](lessons/14_convolutions_on_the_grid/README.md) | ML | Build a CNN, beat the MLP, then articulate why convolution's core assumption is wrong for sudoku. |
| 15 | [Architectures that know about units](lessons/15_constraint_aware_architectures/README.md) | ML | Build the inductive bias in directly: let the network attend along rows, columns and boxes. |
| 16 | [Transformers over 81 tokens](lessons/16_transformers_over_the_grid/README.md) | ML | Treat the grid as a short sequence and let attention learn the constraint structure itself. |
| 17 | [Iterative decoding: the confidence trick](lessons/17_iterative_decoding/README.md) | ML | The pivotal lesson. Stop asking for 81 answers at once; fill the most confident cell, re-run, repeat. |
| 18 | [Loss design and masking](lessons/18_loss_design_and_masking/README.md) | ML | Get the objective right: score only what the model should be predicting. |
| 19 | [Calibration and failure analysis](lessons/19_calibration_and_failure_analysis/README.md) | ML | Find out where and how the model fails, which matters more than its headline number. |

## Stage 3 — Learned search

_Keeping the symbolic solver, learning the decisions inside it._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 20 | [The solver as an environment](lessons/20_solver_as_environment/README.md) | Engineering | Instrument the classical solver so a learned policy can make its decisions. |
| 21 | [Imitation learning for variable ordering](lessons/21_imitation_learning_for_ordering/README.md) | ML | Train a model to copy MRV, confirm it matches, then try to beat the teacher. |
| 22 | [Graph neural networks on the constraint graph](lessons/22_graph_neural_networks/README.md) | ML | Use the actual structure from Lesson 02 as the computation graph. |
| 23 | [Reinforcement learning for heuristic selection](lessons/23_reinforcement_learning/README.md) | ML | Treat 'which heuristic to use at this node' as a decision problem with delayed reward. |
| 24 | [The hybrid solver](lessons/24_neural_guided_search/README.md) | ML | Put it together: symbolic search for correctness, learned policy for speed. Neither alone is enough. |

## Stage 4 — Perception

_Getting a puzzle out of a photograph._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 25 | [Finding the grid in a photograph](lessons/25_classical_cv_pipeline/README.md) | Computer Vision | Classical computer vision, no learning: locate the puzzle and flatten it. |
| 26 | [Cell extraction and empty detection](lessons/26_cell_extraction/README.md) | Computer Vision | Split the warped grid into 81 crops and decide which contain a digit at all. |
| 27 | [Digit classification with MNIST](lessons/27_digit_classification_mnist/README.md) | ML | Train the digit classifier. MNIST is cached locally in `data/raw`, so this works offline. |
| 28 | [The domain gap](lessons/28_the_domain_gap/README.md) | ML | Watch a 99%-accurate MNIST model fall apart on printed puzzle digits, and fix it. |
| 29 | [Synthetic training data](lessons/29_synthetic_image_generation/README.md) | Computer Vision | Render your own puzzle images from generated puzzles, with known labels, entirely offline. |
| 30 | [Photo to solution, end to end](lessons/30_end_to_end_photo_to_solution/README.md) | ML | Assemble the whole pipeline, then confront error propagation -- and use the solver to repair the model. |

## Stage 5 — Difficulty and generation

_Modelling how hard a puzzle is, then building to order._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 31 | [What makes a puzzle hard?](lessons/31_difficulty_proxies/README.md) | Classical AI | Interrogate the difficulty proxies, and find where they disagree with humans. |
| 32 | [Feature-based difficulty regression](lessons/32_feature_based_difficulty/README.md) | ML | Hand-craft features and fit a classical model. Establish the bar a network must clear. |
| 33 | [Learned difficulty from the raw grid](lessons/33_learned_difficulty/README.md) | ML | Predict difficulty from the grid itself and find out whether learned features beat hand-made ones. |
| 34 | [Generating to a target difficulty](lessons/34_conditional_generation/README.md) | ML | Close the loop: generate puzzles that hit a requested difficulty band. |

## Stage 6 — Beyond sudoku

_The same machinery on other constraint problems, including real ones._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 35 | [The same machinery on other puzzles](lessons/35_other_csps/README.md) | Classical AI | Prove the generality: point the solver at problems that are not sudoku. |
| 36 | [SAT encoding](lessons/36_sat_encoding/README.md) | Classical AI | Encode sudoku as boolean satisfiability and hand it to an industrial SAT solver. |
| 37 | [CP-SAT and global constraints](lessons/37_cp_sat_ortools/README.md) | Classical AI | Use a production constraint solver and see what a real `AllDifferent` propagator buys. |
| 38 | [Real constraint problems](lessons/38_scheduling_and_rostering/README.md) | Classical AI | The bridge out of puzzles: the same techniques on problems people pay to have solved. |

## Stage 7 — Deployment

_Shipping a model and being able to reproduce it._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 39 | [Model export and runtime parity](lessons/39_onnx_export/README.md) | Engineering | Get a trained model out of Python and confirm it still gives the same answers. |
| 40 | [Making the model small](lessons/40_quantization_and_distillation/README.md) | ML | Trade accuracy for size and speed deliberately, with the numbers in front of you. |
| 41 | [Running it in the browser](lessons/41_browser_inference_wasm/README.md) | ML | Ship the whole thing as a static page: WASM inference, no server, no upload. |
| 42 | [Reproducibility and experiment tracking](lessons/42_reproducibility_and_tracking/README.md) | Engineering | Make every result in this repo reproducible from a seed and a config. Retrospective, and the most valuable habit here. |

## Stage 8 — Browser and visualisation

_Building the interface: TypeScript, live visualisation, and models in the browser._

| # | Lesson | Kind | Objective |
|---|--------|------|-----------|
| 43 | [Rendering the grid in TypeScript](lessons/43_rendering_the_grid/README.md) | Frontend | Build the 9x9 grid as real DOM with no framework, and learn why the browser is the right place to see a solver think. |
| 44 | [Interaction and state](lessons/44_interaction_and_state/README.md) | Frontend | Make the grid editable and give the user immediate, honest feedback about what they have typed. |
| 45 | [Porting the solver to TypeScript](lessons/45_porting_the_solver/README.md) | Frontend | Reimplement propagation and search in TypeScript, then prove the two implementations agree. |
| 46 | [Visualising constraint propagation](lessons/46_visualising_propagation/README.md) | Frontend | Draw the candidate sets and watch them shrink. This makes Lesson 03 visible rather than abstract. |
| 47 | [Visualising search and backtracking](lessons/47_visualising_search/README.md) | Frontend | Animate the search tree: guesses, propagation cascades, dead ends, and the walk back up. |
| 48 | [Running your model in the browser](lessons/48_model_in_the_browser/README.md) | ML | Load the ONNX model from Stage 7 and run inference client-side, with the classical solver as the correctness backstop. |
| 49 | [Visualising what the model thinks](lessons/49_visualising_the_model/README.md) | ML | Render confidence and attention over the grid. Interpretability is much easier to reason about when you can see it. |
| 50 | [Offline-first deployment](lessons/50_offline_first_deployment/README.md) | Engineering | Ship the whole thing as a static, installable site that works with no network at all. |

name: COMMANDS.md
label: Commands
text:
# Commands

Run everything from the repository root. Once per shell, load the
environment:

```bash
source .env
```

That puts the project virtualenv first on `PATH` — so `python`,
`pytest` and `gridmind` resolve without activating anything — and sets
`GRIDMIND_DEVICE`, `GRIDMIND_SEED` and the other project variables.

This page is generated from `tools/lesson_manifest.py`; regenerate it
with `python tools/scaffold_lessons.py`.

## Checks

Verify the whole stack, no network required:

```bash
gridmind selfcheck
```

```bash
pytest tests -q
```

## The browser app

```bash
scripts/server.sh start
```

Serves at http://localhost:5174. `stop`, `restart`, `status`, `logs`
and `attach` also work; it runs detached, so it survives closing the
terminal. Override the port with `GRIDMIND_PORT`.

## Try the solver

A puzzle that needs real search:

```bash
gridmind solve --puzzle 000000000302540000050301070000000004409006005023054790000000050700810000080060009
```

One that constraint propagation finishes on its own — compare the node
counts:

```bash
gridmind solve --puzzle 000260701680070090190004500820100040004602900050003028009300074040050036703018000
```

```bash
gridmind bench --count 50 --clues 26
```
